h1: Used Audi A6: The 5 Best & Worst Years

contentBlocks.text: Buying a used Audi A6 is always a bit of a risk. When everything is working correctly, it is one of the best cars for long trips because it is fast, comfortable, and full of technology. However, if you pick the wrong year, you might end up spending more on repairs than the car is actually worth.
As a good rule of thumb, avoid the first year of a new generation.
Audi often uses those early models to work out issues with new engines and electronics, and the owners are usually the ones who deal with the consequences:
Older versions are known for catastrophic timing chain problems.
Newer models have had major issues with hybrid systems that can leave you stranded on the highway.

That does not mean you should skip the A6 entirely. If you know which years to look for—like a late C7.5 or a well-maintained C8—you can get a high-end luxury car for a fraction of its original price. To make the choice easier, I looked through recall data and owner reports to find out which years are reliable and which ones are not.
Here are five years of the Audi A6 worth buying, and five that you should probably avoid.
The Best Years to Buy

These are the "sweet spot" years where Audi had already sorted out common mechanical issues, updated the interior tech, and fixed the leaking seals. From the reliable late models of the C7.5 generation to the improved versions of the newer C8, these are the best years to look for if you want an A6 that stays on the road and out of the shop.
● 2018 Audi A6

If you are looking for a used Audi A6, the 2018 model is usually the smartest choice. It was the last year of its generation, so Audi had time to work out the mechanical problems that the earlier versions had. Common issues like leaking water pumps and weak timing chain tensioners were mostly fixed by then, which is why these cars still hold their value so well.

Mechanics usually recommend the 3.0T V6 because of the supercharged engine. It has plenty of power and uses a refined seven-speed transmission that shifts much smoother than the older versions. There is also a 2.0T four-cylinder model, which is actually very reliable because it uses an updated engine design that doesn't burn oil like the older ones did. But if you can afford it, the V6 is the way to go if you want better performance and a car that lasts.
● 2017 Audi A6

If you want to save some money but still get the best features of the C7.5 generation, the 2017 model is a great choice. It is basically the same car as the 2018 version under the hood. You get the same supercharged 3.0T V6 engine and the updated seven-speed transmission, but the price is usually lower just because the car is a year older.

The biggest reason to pick a 2017 over the earlier years is that Audi finally made Apple CarPlay and Android Auto standard. For a daily driver, this makes a huge difference because it keeps the tech feeling modern and means you do not have to use the old factory navigation system. It is a practical way to get the reliability of the C7.5 updates without paying the extra cost for a 2018 model.
● 2022 Audi A6

If you are looking for an Audi A6 with the modern dual-screen interior, the 2022 model is really the best place to start. When Audi first redesigned the A6 in 2019, the early cars had some serious electrical issues. The biggest problem was with the 48-volt hybrid alternator, which would often fail and leave people stranded.

By 2022, Audi had released updated parts and software to fix those hybrid system problems. The touchscreen system is also much more reliable in this version; on the 2019 and 2020 models, the screens would often freeze or just turn black.

One thing to remember is that Audi changed how they name the engines for this generation. The four-cylinder 2.0T is called the 45 TFSI, while the 3.0T V6 is the 55 TFSI. The four-cylinder does the job, but the V6 is much better if you want a true luxury feel and enough power to pass easily on the highway. Choosing a 2022 model lets you get the newer styling and tech without the mechanical headaches that the earlier versions had.
● 2021 Audi A6

Choosing a 2021 model can be a great way to snap up that modern C8 look without spending 2022 money, but you still have to be a little careful. The good news is that by this point, Audi’s software updates finally sorted out those annoying dual-touchscreen freezing issues that drove 2019 and 2020 buyers crazy. The interior tech is way more stable here and actually works like it’s supposed to.

The elephant in the room is still that infamous 48-volt hybrid system, especially if you are hunting for the 3.0T V6 (the 55 TFSI). Those sudden alternator failures that left early buyers stranded on the side of the road were still very much a thing in 2021. If your heart is set on the V6, you absolutely need to dig through the service history to make sure the previous owner had the dealership install the newly revised hybrid generator under warranty. If you want to skip that headache entirely, just look for the 2.0T four-cylinder (the 45 TFSI) instead—it uses a completely different 12-volt setup that doesn't suffer from those sudden electrical meltdowns.
● 2023 Audi A6

If you want a modern C8 Audi A6 and your budget allows for a newer vehicle, the 2023 model is as close to perfect as this generation gets. By this year, all the major headaches that ruined the earlier cars—like the notorious hybrid alternator failures and the glitchy, freezing touchscreens—were completely non-issues straight from the factory. Audi had already standard-issued the updated hardware and stable software.

Another big bonus for 2023 is that Audi made premium driver-assist tech like adaptive cruise control a standard feature. It gives you the exact same modern dual-screen interior and styling as a brand-new showroom model, but at a much smarter used-car price. It is the ultimate "buy-it-and-forget-it" year for the modern generation.
The Worst Years to Avoid

Owning an Audi A6 is a great experience when the car is in good shape, but picking the wrong model year can get expensive fast. Some years are known for having serious problems on the used market. Older models often deal with mechanical issues like burning through too much oil or steering locks, while some newer ones have hybrid systems that can fail while you are driving. If you are looking for a used A6, you should probably stay away from these five specific years.
● 2019 Audi A6

You should probably stay away from the 2019 model. Since it was the first year of the C8 redesign, it basically served as a test run for technology that wasn't quite ready yet. The biggest problem is the 48-volt mild-hybrid system, specifically the starter-generator. This part is known to fail without any warning. When it happens, it can shut down your engine, power steering, and brakes while you are driving, which is obviously a major safety risk. To make matters worse, so many of these have failed that replacement parts are often on backorder for months, leaving owners stranded.

The interior technology is also a constant headache. This was the first year Audi used the dual-touchscreen setup, and the early software is very glitchy. Owners often deal with screens that lag, freeze, or just go black. When that happens, you lose access to your climate controls, navigation, and backup camera. Even if you find one at a low price on the used market, the reliability issues and repair costs make it a bad investment.
● 2020 Audi A6

You should probably skip the 2020 model too. Many buyers think Audi fixed the first-year issues by then, but they didn't. It still has the same 48-volt mild-hybrid system and the same starter-generator problems as the 2019 version. Since Audi hadn't released the improved hardware yet, you still run the risk of the engine and power steering failing unexpectedly while you are driving. On top of that, if the part does fail, you could be waiting months for a replacement because of backorders.

The electronics are also a mess. The infotainment might seem slightly faster than the previous year, but owners still deal with Bluetooth dropping out and Apple CarPlay disconnecting for no reason. The lower screen also tends to freeze up when you are just trying to adjust the AC. It is still a risky and expensive choice if you are looking at the used market.
● 2014 Audi A6

I would stay away from the 2014 model because it has some of the biggest mechanical issues of that whole generation. Even if you go with the smaller 2.0T engine, you aren't really saving yourself from trouble.

Both the 2.0T and 3.0T engines are known for oil problems. While the 3.0T V6 is famous for burning oil and having bad PCV valves, the 2.0T might be even worse. By now, many 2.0T engines have flawed piston rings that make them burn through oil at a crazy rate.

Both engines also have weak timing chain tensioners. On the 2.0T, the chain can stretch and skip, which basically ruins the whole engine. On the 3.0T, fixing a rattling chain requires taking the entire engine out of the car, which costs thousands of dollars just for the labor.

There are other risks too. The 2.0T is prone to turbocharger failures that require replacing the entire unit. Plus, this model year often has issues with the electronic steering rack failing. If that happens while you are driving, the steering suddenly loses all power and becomes very heavy and hard to turn. With all these engine and steering risks, a 2014 A6 is really just a money pit on the used market.
● 2015 Audi A6

The 2015 model is another year that will probably cost you a lot of money in repairs. Even though it is slightly newer than the 2014 version, it has almost all the same mechanical flaws across the entire engine lineup.

With the 3.0T V6, the engine still burns through oil and suffers from water pump and thermostat failures. Since these parts are made of plastic, they often crack and leak coolant. If that happens, the engine can overheat quickly, which can warp the cylinder heads and ruin the engine.

The 2.0T four-cylinder engine has its own expensive risks. These models are known for turbocharger failures and leaks in the high-pressure fuel pump. When the fuel pump leaks internally, gas mixes with the engine oil and thins it out, which causes major internal engine wear. The common problem where the 2.0T uses too much oil is also still present here.

Steering issues from earlier years also carry over. Many drivers report that the steering wheel suddenly becomes very heavy and stiff while driving because the electronic steering rack module fails without warning.
When you consider the high cost of replacing a steering rack and the constant risk of engine damage from leaks, a 2015 A6 is very likely to result in a lot of expensive repair bills.
● 2016 Audi A6

The 2016 model should also be crossed off your list. Many buyers think this year is safe because Audi gave the A6 a facelift, but it just introduced a different set of expensive problems. If you look at the 3.0T V6 engine, it still suffers from bad PCV valves that cause massive oil consumption, and it is notorious for supercharger clutch failures that cause a sudden loss of power when you try to accelerate. Even if you go with the smaller 2.0T four-cylinder engine to save gas, you aren't safe. This year is known for coolant pump leaks that can cause the engine to overheat, and the turbochargers are prone to wastegate rattle or complete failure, which requires replacing the whole turbo.

Beyond the engines, the seven-speed dual-clutch transmission in this model year is a major headache for both versions. Owners frequently complain about the transmission shifting roughly, jerking violently in stop-and-go traffic, or completely throwing error codes on the dash. When these transmissions start to fail, the repair bill at a shop can easily run into thousands of dollars. It might look a bit more modern than the older years, but the combination of engine leaks and transmission glitches makes it a very risky choice on the used market.
Which Audi A6 Should You Actually Buy?

Buying a used Audi A6 can be a good move, but choosing the wrong year can end up costing you a lot of money. You should stay away from the 2019 and 2020 models because they have frequent issues with the hybrid generators and the touchscreens. It is also a good idea to avoid the 2014 through 2016 models, as they often deal with oil burning, steering failures, and expensive transmission problems.

If you want a more reliable version, look for a 2017 or 2018 model. These belong to the late C7.5 generation and have the most dependable engines before the technology became too complex. If you prefer a newer interior and have a higher budget, the 2022 or later models are better options since Audi fixed the earlier software and hybrid issues. No matter which one you choose, always get a pre-purchase inspection from a mechanic before you buy. This helps ensure you get a solid luxury car instead of one that constantly needs repairs.
